screens.title: User Input and Output: Conversing with the Program
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn how a program talks with a person and how a person talks back. The input function pauses the program and returns what the user types as text. That returned text is always a string, even when it looks like a number. We will practice converting that text into numeric values with integer and floating point conversion, and you will see why conversion can fail when the user types unexpected characters. You will also learn how to show results clearly with the print function, how to use separators and the end parameter to control spacing, and how to use formatted strings to create readable numeric output, like currency with two decimal places. Along the way you will study two small interactive examples: a tip calculator and a BMI calculator. These examples illustrate the full input-process-output cycle: prompt the user, parse and compute, then display a friendly result. By the end of the chapter you will understand the common beginner mistakes, why they happen, and how to avoid them with clear prompts and correct conversions.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Conversing with the Program
Interactive 16:9 Masterclass

User Input and Output

Learn how programs pause for input, convert text into numbers for calculations, and print clear results with formatting.

In this lesson
Prompt, parse, compute, and format output with confidence.
Coming up
Examples: tip calculator and BMI calculator. Watch how conversion and formatting affect results and errors.
Why this matters

Interactive programs are more useful and human-friendly. Correct conversion prevents runtime errors and ensures calculations are accurate and presentable.

Concept Map
Prompt
A clear question shown to the user so they know what to type.
Raw Input
Always text. Even digits arrive as characters.
Conversion
Use integer or floating conversions before math.
Output
Print results using separators or formatted strings for clarity.
Explore Key Topics
input function
Pauses for user text and returns a string.
Conversion
Use int or float when you need numbers.
Formatting
F-strings and format specifiers like two decimals for money.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to read text from a user, convert that text into numbers when you need to compute, and present results clearly. First, you will learn to use the input function to pause a program and collect a prompt response. Second, you will learn that the input function always returns text, and why that matters when you perform arithmetic. Third, you will practice converting text to integers and floating point numbers for calculations, and see when conversions can fail. Fourth, you will learn to print results in readable formats, using argument separation, end characters, and formatted strings with numeric precision. Each objective builds practical skill: reading input makes programs interactive; recognizing string results prevents type errors; converting input enables calculations; and formatting output improves clarity for users. You will practice with a tip calculator and a BMI example so you can apply these skills immediately. These objectives prepare you for error handling and conditionals in later chapters.

screens.title: Learning Objectives — Practice & Mistakes
screens.narratorSegment: These objectives also teach you how mistakes happen so you can avoid them. You'll practice reading input and converting it with concrete examples: asking for a name, an age, a price, or a temperature. You will see why trying arithmetic directly on text leads to errors and how to fix those errors with explicit conversion. You will also learn how to craft prompts that reduce mistakes by telling the user exactly what is expected. Finally, you'll practice formatting output so results are readable and professional. Each practice ties to a concrete example: greeting a user by name, computing a birthday year from an integer age, converting Celsius to Fahrenheit using floating conversions, and formatting money with two decimals in an f-string. As you practice, notice one common error: assuming input gives a number. That misconception produces a type error at runtime. Recognizing that assumption is the first step to writing correct interactive programs.

Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Practice & Mistakes

Practice & Common Mistakes

Example: greeting
Ask for a name and print a greeting. This shows how input returns text you can reuse directly for display.
Example: age mistake
If you ask for age and then add 1 without converting, you will get a type error. Always convert before arithmetic.
Mnemonic
Prompt clearly, parse immediately, then process. Prompt → Parse → Process.
Why it matters
Clear prompts and early conversion prevent runtime errors and make programs predictable for users.

screens.title: The input function: pause and return text
screens.narratorSegment: The input function pauses program execution and waits for the user to type a response. The most important rule to remember is that the returned value is text, also called a string. That means digits, letters, or symbols typed by the user arrive as characters inside a string value. A typical pattern is assigning the returned text to a variable and then using that variable for display or conversion. For example, asking for a name and then greeting the person uses that text directly. A common misconception is to assume typing numbers automatically gives numeric values. If you ask for age and think you can add one to the returned value without converting, the program will fail because you are trying to perform arithmetic on text. In practice, write a clear prompt with a space at the end so the cursor is visible and choose variable names that describe the content. Use a prompt that hints at format when required, for instance asking for weight in kilograms or height in meters. Clear prompts reduce invalid responses and make later conversion simpler. Now try thinking about what the user will type before you write the prompt.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Input Function
Core Concept

input pauses and returns text

Use prompts to ask the user for data. The result is always a string, so plan to convert if you need numbers.

Concrete example
Ask for a name like first name only. The program stores the typed characters and you can print a greeting directly with that text.
Common mistake
Assuming numbers are numeric. If you try math on text, you will get a type error.
Prompt Design
A good prompt is specific and ends with a space so the cursor is not jammed. Include units when relevant, for example ask for weight in kilograms or temperature in Celsius.
Try this mentally
  • Imagine asking for a price. What hint would you include so the user types numbers and not words?
  • Think about acceptable formats: decimals, commas, or currency symbols.
Key Takeaway

The input function returns text; design prompts to guide the user and prepare for conversion.

screens.title: Text versus Number: why input returns a string
screens.narratorSegment: Input returns text because keyboards and terminals produce characters. Treating that returned value as a number without conversion is a common source of beginner errors. When you receive '25' as text and try to add one, the program cannot mix text and numeric types and raises a type error. One way to see the difference is to explicitly check the type after reading input. Converting to an integer or floating point value changes the stored type so arithmetic works. A useful classroom analogy is a letter in an envelope: the input function hands you the envelope containing characters. Conversion is like opening the envelope and turning the characters into a number that math understands. A misconception to watch for is assuming that digits typed by the user are automatically numeric. That assumption leads to runtime failure. For now, assume users follow the prompt format. Later we will handle invalid cases with error handling. Practically, write code that converts input immediately when you expect numbers; this makes the rest of the code simpler and safer. Text versus Number: why input returns a string means strings and numbers are different types; convert strings to numbers before performing arithmetic to avoid typeerror.. In practical terms, understand the type difference and the resulting errors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Text vs Number
Definition

Why input returns text

Key point: keyboards produce characters. Input captures those characters as a string. Even digits are characters until you convert them.

Analogy
Think of input as handing you an envelope with characters inside. Conversion opens it and interprets the contents as a number.
Quick check
If you see a TypeError when adding, ask yourself: did I convert the input to a number?
Concrete example
name = input('What is your name? ')
print('Hello,', name)

age = input('How old are you? ')  # user types: 25
print(type(age))  # shows string

# Wrong: next_year = age + 1  # TypeError
This example shows the type check and the error when arithmetic is attempted on text.

screens.title: Convert input to numbers: int and float
screens.narratorSegment: When your program needs to compute using user-supplied values, convert the text immediately to the numeric type you need. Use integer conversion when you expect whole numbers and floating point conversion when decimals are possible. The pattern is straightforward: prompt the user, convert the returned text using integer or floating conversion, then perform the calculation. Converting early keeps the rest of your code simple because subsequent operations assume numeric types. A concrete example: asking for age can call integer conversion so you can add one to compute next year. For temperatures you should use floating conversion because Celsius might include decimals. Remember conversions can fail if the user types letters or incorrectly formatted numbers. For now, assume valid input, but plan to learn error handling soon. A good mental checklist: confirm expected format in the prompt, convert immediately, and use variables that reflect the numeric type to avoid confusion. This approach reduces type-related bugs and makes your calculations reliable. Convert input to numbers: int and float means prompt → convert with int or float → compute. convert early to keep later code numeric-friendly.. In practical terms, when and how to convert user text into numeric types. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Convert to Numbers
Process

Steps to convert and compute

1.
Prompt the user with a clear message including expected format and units.
2.
Convert immediately using integer conversion for whole numbers or floating conversion for decimals.
3.
Compute using the numeric variables and then format results for display.
Example
age = int(input('How old are you? '))
next_year = age + 1
print('Next year you will be', next_year)
Key Takeaway

Convert user text to the numeric type you need right after input to avoid mixing types later.

When to use float

Use floating conversion for measurements and currency where decimals happen, such as temperature and bill amounts.

Example: temperature
temperature = float(input('Enter the temperature in Celsius: '))
fahrenheit = temperature * 9 / 5 + 32
print(f'That is {fahrenheit} degrees Fahrenheit.')
Misconception
Converting later in code can hide errors. Convert early so the rest of the program works with numbers, not text.

screens.title: Handling invalid input: ValueError and assumptions
screens.narratorSegment: Conversion functions can fail when the text provided cannot be interpreted as a number. When integer or floating conversion sees letters or malformed numbers it raises a value error. For example, converting the word 'abc' to a number will not work. In this chapter we simplify by assuming users follow prompts and enter valid input. That assumption lets us focus on the mechanics of conversion and formatting. However, in real programs you must handle invalid input using error handling and repeated prompts until valid data is provided. The immediate learning objective is to recognize the failure mode and avoid it by writing clear prompts. Asking for a number and including an example format in the prompt reduces mistakes. When you later learn try and except, you will wrap conversions so the program can respond gracefully instead of crashing. For now, practice writing prompts and converting input, and be mindful that conversion functions are strict: they expect a properly formatted digit sequence for integers and a number format for floating conversion. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › Invalid Input
ValueError

When conversion fails

If a user types non-numeric text where a number is expected, integer and floating conversions will raise an error. Recognize this failure mode and plan to address it later.

Example failure
age = int(input('How old are you? '))  # user types: abc
# raises ValueError
Practical tip
Write clear prompts that include units and format hints to reduce invalid responses.
Future skill
Later you will use try and except to catch conversion failures and ask the user again without crashing.
Key Takeaway

Expect conversions to be strict; until you add error handling, assume the user follows the prompt format.

screens.title: print: multiple arguments, sep and end
screens.narratorSegment: The print function is flexible and helpful for shaping output. It accepts multiple arguments and prints them separated by a space by default. You can change that separator with the sep parameter when you want a different divider between values, for example a vertical bar. The end parameter controls what print appends at the end: by default it is a newline, but you can set it to an empty string to continue the next printed text on the same line. Combining sep and end gives you precise control over spacing and line breaks. A common usage pattern is printing labels with values by passing several arguments rather than building long concatenated strings. For formatted numeric output, though, f-strings provide both readability and format control. In practice, use multiple print arguments for simple labels and use f-strings when you need numeric formatting such as fixed decimal places. Notice that print never changes variable types; it only displays values. Practice reading examples and predicting the output before running code to build intuition. print: multiple arguments, sep and end means use multiple print arguments with sep for separators and end to control line endings; combine with f-strings for formatted values.. In practical terms, control spacing and line endings for clean output. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › print & Formatting
Code Walkthrough

Multiple arguments and separators

name = 'Alice'
age = 25
print('Name:', name, 'Age:', age)
print('Name:', name, sep=' | ')
print('Loading', end='')
print('...', end='')
print('Done!')
Predict the printed lines: the first shows labels and values separated by spaces; the second uses a custom separator; the last three prints combine to form 'Loading...Done!'.
Why it matters

Small formatting choices make output easier to read. Use separators for quick labels and end to avoid unwanted newlines during progress indicators.

Pro tip
For polished numeric output, prefer formatted strings rather than manual concatenation of values.
Key Takeaway

Use print arguments, sep, and end to structure output; use f-strings when you need formatted numbers.

screens.title: F-strings and numeric formatting
screens.narratorSegment: Formatted strings, often called f-strings, let you embed expressions directly inside a string template and control numeric formatting. This feature makes output readable and concise. For example, when you calculate a price times quantity, an f-string can include the multiplication result and a format specifier to show two decimal places, which is essential for currency. The format specifier uses a colon, a period, and a precision number; in practice you will write something that displays two decimals for monetary values. F-strings evaluate expressions inside the template, so you can write the calculation inline and avoid temporary variables when appropriate. A frequent beginner question is whether formatting changes the underlying value — it does not. Formatting only controls how the number is displayed. Use formatting to avoid long floats like 3.0000000004 and present friendly results. As you practice, try combining f-strings with conversions so the final printed value is both numeric and well formatted. F-strings and numeric formatting means use f-strings to embed expressions and format numeric output, such as two decimal places for prices.. In practical terms, embed expressions and format numbers to two decimal places. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 02 › Chapter 2.4 › F-strings
Code Walkthrough

Embedding expressions and formatting

item = 'apple'
price = 0.75
quantity = 4
print(f'You bought {quantity} {item}s for ${price * quantity:.2f}')
# Output: You bought 4 apples for $3.00
The specifier after a colon controls display. For two decimal places, use a dot and the number of decimals. The raw numeric value stays unchanged; only the printed representation is rounded for display.
Common confusion
Formatting does not alter the stored number. If you need a rounded value for calculation, explicitly round the number in a separate step.

screens.title: Tip Calculator: full input-process-output example
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the tip calculator to see the entire input-process-output cycle. The program first prints a title so the user knows what it does. It then prompts for the bill amount and tip percentage, converting both inputs to floating point numbers because cents and fractional percentages are possible. The computation multiplies the bill by the tip percentage divided by one hundred to compute the tip amount, then adds the tip to the bill to get the total. Finally, the program prints both tip and total using formatted strings with two decimals so money appears correctly. This example demonstrates practical choices: float conversion for monetary values, inline arithmetic for clarity, and f-strings for readable currency. Note the program assumes valid input. If the user types letters when asked for numeric values, the conversion will raise an error. Review the code mentally and predict the printed lines before running it, then try editing the tip percentage to see how the output changes. In practical terms, read numbers, compute tip, and format the results. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

It then prompts for the bill amount and tip percentage, converting both inputs to floating point numbers because cents and fractional percentages are possible. screens.title: Prompt design and best practices
screens.narratorSegment: Well-crafted prompts are one of the simplest defenses against invalid input. A good prompt is specific, includes units, and shows an example of valid input when helpful. For instance, ask for height in meters and include a sample like zero point seven five to indicate decimals, or ask for price with a dollar sign and state whether cents are allowed. Always include a trailing space in the prompt so the user's cursor does not appear glued to the text. Use variable names that reflect the expected type, for example bill_amount or height_meters, so your code is self-documenting. When you have many prompts, grouping related prompts together with a short title helps the user understand context. These small choices reduce the chance of value errors and make future error handling easier. When we add try and except, these prompts will work together with validation to create robust, user-friendly interactive programs. In this lesson you will learn how a program talks with a person and how a person talks back. The input function pauses the program and returns what the user types as text. That returned text is always a string, even when it looks like a number. We will practice converting that text into numeric values with integer and floating point conversion, and you will see why conversion can fail when the user types unexpected characters. You will also learn how to show results clearly with the print function, how to use separators and the end parameter to control spacing, and how to use formatted strings to create readable numeric output, like currency with two decimal places. Along the way you will study two small interactive examples: a tip calculator and a BMI calculator. These examples illustrate the full input-process-output cycle: prompt the user, parse and compute, then display a friendly result. By the end of the chapter you will understand the common beginner mistakes, why they happen, and how to avoid them with clear prompts and correct conversions.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to read text from a user, convert that text into numbers when you need to compute, and present results clearly. First, you will learn to use the input function to pause a program and collect a prompt response. Second, you will learn that the input function always returns text, and why that matters when you perform arithmetic. Third, you will practice converting text to integers and floating point numbers for calculations, and see when conversions can fail. Fourth, you will learn to print results in readable formats, using argument separation, end characters, and formatted strings with numeric precision. Each objective builds practical skill: reading input makes programs interactive; recognizing string results prevents type errors; converting input enables calculations; and formatting output improves clarity for users. You will also learn how to craft prompts that reduce mistakes by telling the user exactly what is expected. Finally, you'll practice formatting output so results are readable and professional. Each practice ties to a concrete example: greeting a user by name, computing a birthday year from an integer age, converting Celsius to Fahrenheit using floating conversions, and formatting money with two decimals in an f-string. As you practice, notice one common error: assuming input gives a number. That misconception produces a type error at runtime.
